ChIJ0X-jggVTaYcR1cUs8hH36SU.home: After many wonderful years of celebrating love stories, I wanted to share an exciting update about the future of our venue. As many of you know, I will be retiring in October 2026. My remaining wedding dates through October are fully booked, and I am no longer accepting additional bookings before my retirement. I'm happy to share that the venue will continue welcoming couples under new ownership beginning in November 2026. While it will be a completely new business with a new name and owner, the venue will continue serving couples who dream of celebrating their special day here. The new owner is now accepting bookings for weddings taking place in November 2026 and throughout 2027 and beyond. If you've been hoping to celebrate your wedding at this beautiful venue after my retirement, you'll still have that opportunity with the new business, rebranded as McCreery Gardens. Visit their website at www.coweddingvenue.com or reach out via email by contacting info@coweddingvenue.com It has been an incredible privilege to be part of so many unforgettable wedding days, and I am deeply grateful to every couple and family who entrusted me with such an important milestone. Thank you for allowing me to do what I have loved for so many years. I'm excited to see this special place begin its next chapter, and I know it will continue to be a beautiful setting where new memories are made for years to come. Thank you all for your continued support, kindness, and encouragement throughout the years. It has truly meant the world to me. ❤️ An Enchanting Place that feels like Home... The McCreery House is a Nationally Registered Historic Home nestled in the Sweetheart City of Loveland CO. Built in the 1890's it was historically known as the Showplace of Loveland. ChIJ0X-jggVTaYcR1cUs8hH36SU.about: William H. McCreery originally built the house. He was born in the Ligonier Valley, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania on November 17, 1839. He attended Military school in Pennsylvania and became ordained as a Presbyterian Minister. In 1870 he married his first wife Martha Marshall. In 1874 they came to Colorado seeking to improve his health and a chance to start a church of his faith in the wilderness. Mr. McCreery traveled up and down the eastern slope of the mountains looking for a place for a second congregation of the United Presbyterian Church. He was invited to Alexander Canyon (now Big Thompson Canyon) and decided that this is where he wanted to begin his work. The United Presbyterian Church of Loveland was born on Thanksgiving Day, the 25th of November 1875. It is said that Rev. McCreery preached a sermon from Psalm 105. In its first years the church met in schoolhouses. The first church building was completed on August 1, 1878, and located on Fourth Street and Lincoln. This church cost $1600 to build and the Board of Church Extension loaned $600 of the money. In 1879 he discontinued his pastoral duties and retired to his farm. He was appointed superintendent of schools in 1882 for Larimer County and held this position for 5 years. In 1888 McCreery conducted the Loveland Academy for advanced students. Your design and dress can be flawless, but when it comes to the emotional story, “perfect” doesn’t exist, and it would be boring if it did. All our best memories are usually the unexpected ones. Creating an illusion of perfection actually misses the real and honest moments that make for incredible photographs – the ones you’ll relive for decades to come. For me, a perfect story is authentic, vulnerable, and engaging. It’s evergreen images you can’t stop looking at because they make you feel everything. Unplanned moments. The almost-missed nuances. The moments no one else saw coming. The way you smile when your fiancé sees you for the first time. These are the experiences I capture – never missing a single detail. It’s you, as you’ve never seen yourself before . “ I am absolutely obsessed with our photographs from our wedding day. It is extremely easy to relive it by simply looking at our photographs. Jenna captured emotion in our photos that I did not think was possible. ” I capture moments that speak for themselves. From the second you lock eyes, to your father’s single shedded tear, to the wild wedding party – every moment, just like you, is unique and beautiful. I want the small moments to speak volumes and the big moments to grow quiet and still. My job as an artist is to capture the seconds that no one else sees, and to portray the real you through masterful photography. “ Not only is Jenna a talented photographer, she is also a wonderful soul. ChIJ5__npftya4cR-3EqxtNSofw.about: For nearly a century, Meadow Creek has been a place where people gather, retreat, and reconnect with one another. What began as a mountain homestead evolved into an inn and bed-and-breakfast, and today is a destination for weddings, celebrations, and weekends shared with close friends and family. The first homestead patent was granted in 1927, and a modest 10-by-10 log cabin was built on the property. At the time, Pine was a rugged mountain community connected by logging roads, ranchland, and small settlements. That original cabin still stands today as a reminder of the property's earliest beginnings. In 1931, Italian Prince Balthasar Gialma Odescalchi and his wife, Denver native Elaine Wilcox, purchased the property and transformed the homestead into a private mountain ranch. Together they constructed the stone lodge and many of the supporting buildings that remain today. Using locally quarried granite from the property and regional timber, they created a retreat that felt deeply connected to the surrounding landscape. Nearly a century later, the craftsmanship and materials continue to define Meadow Creek's character. For nearly forty years, Meadow Creek was home to the Douglass family. The first video advertisement came to us by Bulova in 1941. It ran for 10 seconds on a billboard during a baseball game for just $9.00. And it’s pretty, yawwwn. Advertisements have come a long way since then, from the way we understand human psychology to the technology and expertise available today. But it really wasn’t very long after the 40’s that marketers learned the power of targeting their customers with storytelling ads. Storytelling uses a combination of elements, like characters, setting, and plot to build a narrative. In advertising, marketing professionals use those key components to develop relatable stories that connect with their ideal customers. Companies started creating storytelling ads by casting people who looked like those they were marketing their products to in settings that were familiar to them. Think housewives presenting refrigerators and stoves in their 1950s homes. ChIJ75ssAQKSbIcReLM-YNsepYw.about: Truth is, little is known about this magnificent estate and its grounds except that it was built in the 1970s. Historical records of the Villa’s inception were destroyed in a fire at the local county courthouse in 1978. The purchase, permits, and construction of the Villa were lost. We do know the original owner was of Italian descent, but why he created this feast of Mediterranean architecture in the heart of Colorado remains a mystery. And so, this beautiful enclave, which boasts no aging documents of its pedigree, seems to have written its own history- one of celebration, tinkling toasts, and the promise of love. Oh, the many occasions that these walls have commemorated! The Villa’s lovely rooms and elegant halls have soaked up the joy of brides and grooms, wit of businessmen and women, adorning families, and countless moments of gaiety and a million heartfelt laughs. Its legacy is captured in wedding albums and partakers’ memories. The Villa Parker’s history is one of families, co-workers, and friends who have come together for great occasions. Its story unfolds with each sweet moment of celebration.

Maybe their furry friend had the best puppy dog eyes or maybe the 2 year old had that sassy face you know will go away someday. The beauty of pictures is it stops time, for just a little while. Kids grow up and many things in life change. But that's the best part - we get to celebrate the here and now! Some of my favorite pictures, both professionally and personally are sweet moments that have nothing to do with clothing choices or detailed planning. So don't over-think it! My approach is to ACTUALLY have fun, enjoy the process AND get great photos. I want you to look at your walls and see great pictures! Jen completely blew us away with her choice of location for our photos! She knows where to find unique hidden away gems that made our photos timeless. She is so easy to work with and so kind! We brought our dog along for the photos. Jen did an amazing job capturing his personality along with our family! Our family photos turned out beautiful - I couldn’t recommend her more! Jen is an absolute pleasure and a delight to work with. She has such an artistic eye, and a true passion for photography and it shows in the quality of her pictures. My work is rooted in observation: the way natural light moves through a room, how materials soften or deepen in response, and the subtle relationships between texture, shape, and space. Photographing interiors feels like a natural extension of this way of seeing. Randy and Cheryl Miller purchased the building and grounds in 1996 as the site for their business, Randall’s Photography. ChIJMQnlDWj7a4cR7TXJWZ7nNg4.about: In the summer of 1965, my dad, Wally, and I spent countless hours driving the dusty roads between Boulder and Fort Collins. Wally was on a mission—to find the perfect place to raise cattle and teach his kids about the joys of country living. Just outside the town of Hygiene, 45 miles from Denver, we found it: a little slice of heaven we named Crane Hollow Farm. Wally followed his dream, raising cattle for years, including a few Grand Champion Bulls. But more than that, he passed down a love for the simple, meaningful things—like playing in the mud and connecting with the land. When it came time for me to teach my own kids about country life, I embraced it wholeheartedly. I encouraged them to explore the fields, splash in the pond, and embrace the beauty of the outdoors. So, when my eldest daughter asked to be married at The Farm, I couldn’t have been prouder. Crane Hollow Farm is more than a place—it’s an experience. We love it for its stunning views of Longs Peak and the Rocky Mountains, the pond, the fields, the cows, and the horses. We treasure the moments spent around the campfire, the fresh country air, and the joy of gathering with friends and family far from the city’s hustle. ChIJLUtw-tl-bIcRRTDggnRUmGI.home: A Place Of Historical Elegance For Your Event The Mansion, located at 770 Pennsylvania Street in Denver's Quality Hill neighborhood, offers an elegant setting weddings, receptions, holiday parties, meetings and retreats. Celebrate your next special event with us and let us help you make memories that last a lifetime. Take your place in history! Perched on Quality Hill in the heart of Denver, the Grant-Humphreys Mansion was built in 1902 in a Beaux-Arts style commissioned by James Benton Grant, the third Governor of Colorado, and his wife, the prominent socialite Mary Goodell Grant. In 1917, Mary sold the mansion to another influential and connected family, the Humphreys, best remembered for opening Denver’s first airport. For more than half a century, the Grant-Humphreys Mansion played host to the elegant soirées of Colorado’s elite. In 1976, it was bequeathed by Ira Boyd Humphreys to the Colorado Historical Society (now History Colorado), so that future generations of Coloradans could continue to enjoy this sumptuous setting for their own special occasions.

ChIJO5gjyJ5-bIcRokJMcq8KM0Y.about: After WWII, Weldon Newberry and two of his brothers purchased a greenhouse on Garfield Street in Denver, Colorado. In 1950, the Newberry brothers purchased an additional greenhouse in Littleton, Colorado which was given to the youngest Newberry brother. A few years later, Weldon and his wife, Elizabeth, purchased full ownership from the remaining brother. With fuel prices skyrocketing, carnations were being shipped into the United States for cheaper than they could be grown in the greenhouse. At this point, the greenhouses were used to grow a large variety of flowers and plants and Elizabeth Newberry focused on developing the wedding party and floral side of the business. The daughter of Weldon and Elizabeth Newberry, Paula Newberry-Arnold, now co-owns the business with her son. She has developed the business into one of Denver’s top floral and decor shops specializing in a variety of large themed events and daily custom floral designs. Cooper has a love for music that speaks to him, plus a love for jerseys. ChIJOzLZXtN-bIcRk-PyUZj4Tpw.title: Denver Catholic Photographers | A&D Creative
ChIJOzLZXtN-bIcRk-PyUZj4Tpw.desc: Denver Catholic wedding photographers Anya and Dan are a husband-wife team based in Colorado who specialize in capturing Catholic weddings.
ChIJOzLZXtN-bIcRk-PyUZj4Tpw.home: We are a wife-and-husband team of photographers who love the outdoors and telling stories with our cameras, capturing organic moments with beautiful, natural light against stunning backdrops. We met as 22-year-old journalists in a newsroom in 2009, started our business, dated and eventually married in 2013. We’re blessed with a wonderful life and home in the Washington Park neighborhood of Denver. We love capturing amazing pictures of couples throughout Colorado, and we hope to tell your story, too. We are photographers, journalists, writers, adventurers, voracious readers and parents to two spunky toddlers. We met in a newsroom copy room. Anya was a newly hired editorial assistant, prepping documents for an afternoon meeting; Dan was a summer news intern. The copy room, also home to employee mail boxes, gave Dan the perfect excuse to “randomly” bump into Anya as she collected fresh paper printouts, still warm from the copier. That day in September 2009 launched us on an unexpected path. Though our love story didn’t take shape for many months to come, the shared passion for storytelling and journalism we recognized in each other that day would provide the foundation for a friendship, business, and marriage. We carry the spirit of journalism we cultivated there into everything we photograph. We want to capture the real, unscripted moments. We want to bear witness and document the event fully. Beauty can be found in the in between, and that’s what we strive to capture. The History and Renovation of the D-Barn: The Dickens/Lashley Barn was built approximately 1916 by Senator Theodore Lashley. The barn was used as a dairy barn for part of its long history. It was converted into storage in its more recent history. In March of 1996 Sue Connelly, a D-Barn owner, attended a Chamber of Commerce ground breaking ceremony at the site where the barn used to sit at 5th and Lashley. The barn was slated for the dump to make way for a new affordable housing complex. Six weeks later the barn was moved, all in one piece, to the present site. Since then the barn has undergone extensive renovation. The old shingles were removed and the entire barn power washed. The old flooring was removed and used on the end walls. A new 2" x 6" tongue and groove floor was installed. The barn has been insulated from top to bottom. Air conditioning and 5 zone heating was installed. This structure is designated a historic structure by The City of Longmont and Boulder County. "How do you spell love? You don't spell it, you feel it." ChIJa7Z9VHR4a4cRdUpG_WjJ3uU.about: Willow Ridge Manor was built as a family home in 1911. It was located on a farm close to present-day Kipling and Bear Creek. It was featured in a publication of the Lakewood Historical Society with this description; "Extensively remodeled from a pre-existing dwelling into this Colonial-style mansion by George Allen in 1915. Allen's home and Kendalvue Farm occupied historical land. Joseph Rist of Pennsylvania, lumberman and grain raiser, acquired acreage near the home's site in 1865 and probably built and named Pennsylvania House, a stage stop on South Kipling street at Bear Creek. The property was later acquired by another pioneer, Henry Teller, 30 years United States Senator [representing Colorado] and Secretary of the Interior in President Chester Arthur's cabinet. This home was also the residence of Watt Redfield, the inventor of the Redfield gunsight." In the 1980s the farm was re-developed for housing units and the mansion fell into disrepair. But a group of people rescued the mansion from demolition by moving it to its present location, surrounded by red rock formations, south of the town of Morrison. They then breathed new life into the mansion by re-purposing it into a unique wedding ceremony and reception venue. ChIJbZBhXh-ba4cRH1Nbz-Vw8wk.about: This isn’t just the story of the collection of buildings that are the Buffalo Rose that we know today. It isn’t a story about wood, brick, steel, fire and stone— not simply a tale of the many businesses that have stood on the site or the colorful characters that have passed through these doors. No, this is the story of Golden City, one of Colorado’s very first municipalities and where our great state has its roots. It is the story of the American West and a rugged frontier spirit. It is a story about architecture and governments, railroads, cars, and motorcycles; shootouts, Olympians, entrepreneurs, and wars— it is a story of great economic expansion and profound depression, of drunken debauchery and of Prohibition. This is the story of The Buffalo Rose, but more importantly for the people of Golden, Colorado: it is Our Story. The properties comprising the present day Buffalo Rose have been the pulse of Golden since the City’s founding in 1859. Golden has grown up around the site and the businesses located at the bustling corner of Washington Avenue and 12th Street have provided the commercial lifeblood of the town for well over 150 years! ChIJdeqz6jB8a4cRBra7YFv5uI0.about: The Kathryn Kalmbach Herbarium of Vascular Plants (KHD), Sam Mitchel Herbarium of Fungi (DBG), and Denver Botanic Gardens Arthropod Collection (DBGA) are an integral part of the Gardens. Our natural history collections document vascular plants and fungi from the Southern Rocky Mountain Region, as well as insect, spider, and greater arthropod diversity within the Gardens. At their core, these collections capture species diversity and distribution. Not only do these collections hold precious evidence of how landscapes and populations change overtime – they are also physical time capsules of genetics and morphology. In 2020, our collections moved from the lower level of Boettcher Memorial Center to the ground level of the Freyer – Newman Center , which allows them to expand in size and in accessibility to researchers and the public. Twelve Days Without Medical Care: A Fight for Survival In 2016, while serving time inside a detention facility, Kareem accidentally struck his head against a bottom bunk. The impact caused a subdural hematoma, a severe brain bleed that pooled blood between his brain and skull. Despite suffering from excruciating physical trauma, Kareem's urgent requests for emergency care were repeatedly ignored by jail medical personnel. For twelve agonizing days, he remained confined without proper treatment while his condition steadily deteriorated. The striking results highlight the craftsmanship of Building Restoration Specialties (BRS). The restored north, east, south, and west elevations now feature cleaned and repaired stonework that appears significantly lighter and more vibrant than the adjoining bell tower, which was not included in this project’s scope. This project was made possible thanks to generous support from the State Historical Fund , ensuring that this iconic Highlands landmark continues to be a source of pride and beauty for the community. Thank you to Historic Denver’s John Deffenbaugh, Jay Homstad, and most especially Mike Owen for your guidance, support, and partnership. Thank you to Elizabeth, Fernando, Bart, and Rhonda at BRS— you’re class acts and a pleasure to work with! And last but not least, thank you to the people of Colorado and our great neighbors who call Highland home! I recently had a friend shoot photos of my family when I found out my dad had cancer. He passed soon after, and those photos are now the most precious things in the world to me. ChIJmb86Je15bIcRP8jYOipyG1Y.about: Today, the reimagined Apollo Hall pays tribute to its colorful past while standing as a vibrant reminder of Denver's pioneer spirit and the remarkable transformation of Larimer Square. Apollo Hall, located at 1427 Larimer Street , has a storied history that mirrors the evolution of Larimer Square and Denver itself. Originally built in the 1800s by Barney Bros & Co. as a billiard and liquor saloon, it quickly transformed into Denver's first conveniently located hotel and then, by October 1859, into a lively theater. Known for its drinking, gambling, and theatrical performances on the second floor, Apollo Hall also served various purposes over the years, including a courtroom, lighting store, and furniture shop. By the mid-20th century, like much of Larimer Square , the building had fallen into decline. However, Dana Crawford’s preservation efforts in the 1960s revitalized the area, restoring its Victorian charm and historical significance.

ChIJnbAyyzVocEARQIunn893gtM.about: The Barn at Evergreen Memorial Park is a remarkable assembly of five historic barns from the local Evergreen & Conifer area. Each barn, ranging from seventy to one hundred years old at the time of its build in 1999, contributed a piece of itself to create what we have as our barn today. The Barn now rests on the beautiful mountain property originally purchased as a private park in 1965 by Ron and Carol Lewis. Ron and Carol committed the 100-acre site as a tribute to the pioneers of Evergreen and the Old West, creating what is now known as Evergreen Memorial Park. Most of the land is used as a private animal ranch. Buffalo, elk, yak, fallow deer, goats, chickens, ducks, geese, owls, foxes, horses, and one particularly faithful migrant heron occupy the property. As well as protecting wildlife, the Lewises strive to preserve the pioneer heritage of the Old West at Evergreen Memorial Park. They established several large garden areas on the high plains meadows where restored stone and timber cabins have been preserved. The six distinct and separate garden areas now serve as a cemetery and the final resting place for many Colorado natives. Buildings slated for destruction have been refurbished, and wagons, tractors and plows, discovered on neighboring ranches, act to remind visitors of the era when Jefferson County was once considered the potato capital of Colorado. ChIJn6VwawF5a4cRALO0pSVaMSU.about: OCTOBER 17,1914 – John Charles Shaffer purchased the first 2,660 acres of what would become the Ken-Caryl Ranch for $100,000. He and his wife, Virginia Conser Shaffer (1850 – 1932), named it Ken-Caryl after their sons, Kent and Carroll. John Charles Shaffer (1852 – 1943) was born in Baltimore. He arrived in Chicago in 1874 where he worked as a grain commission trader. A few years later he purchased his first street railway company, in Richmond, Indiana. From there he purchased street car lines in Indianapolis and Chicago. In 1901 he purchased the Chicago Evening Post newspaper and from there went on to acquire a string of newspapers in the Midwest. After visiting his son, Kent, who was living in Denver, in 1913 Shaffer expanded his empire with the purchase of the Rocky Mountain News, the Denver Times, and the Denver Republican newspapers. The Denver Times reported that “Mr. Shaffer gave instructions for the drawing of plans for a summer home modeled on the colonial style, to cost approximately $100,000. This building will be situated on the highest portion of the estate and is prophesied to become the nucleus of a colony of summer retreats for millionaires.” He immediately commissioned the architect Edbrooke, famous for his work on the Brown Palace, Oxford Hotel and many other prominent Denver buildings. Founded our nonprofit initiative to preserve Indigenous wisdom and unite the tribes. Long-term partnerships defining our practice — value delivered consistently over years. The Indigo Project is our nonprofit initiative. Beyond preservation, Indigo convenes a global roundtable uniting leadership from Indigenous, old- and new-world tribes around three questions: How can Indigenous wisdom heal humanity, save Mother Earth, and prevent the parasitic colonialism of the cosmos? Reconciling with Indigenous peoples and their critical connection to nature. Global equity & the age of post-scarcity. h2: Making art out of your love. Soulful documentation on film and digital.
ChIJy1gQkput0ysRtxNXH884ntw.home: Making art out of your love. Soulful documentation on film and digital. A film wedding photographer based in Denver, Colorado. I like to think of myself as a photojournalist who just happens to shoot weddings. The images I make will be a reflection of you, your story, and the things and the people that matter most to you, all captured artfully and intentionally, with the ultimate goal of uncovering the soul of your day. This is what makes my pictures so unique, and why capturing wedding days is my favorite thing in the world. I live for the chaos just as much as I’m inspired by the mundane. Wedding days are the ultimate culmination of life and love. They are the one day in your entire life where all of your favorite people are going to be in one place to celebrate you . This amalgamation of people, emotions, and experiences is so fun and interesting to me. I love how raw, messy, and real wedding days are. This is why I love photographing weddings—because I love photographing life . And real life happens at weddings. My work reflects this messiness. It’s fun, it’s honest, it’s alive . I work with couples who value the chaos; who don’t feel the need to perform for my camera. So that when it comes to telling the story of your wedding day, I’m able to step back, observe, and simply make art—like a friend who just so happens to be good with a camera.
ChIJy1gQkput0ysRtxNXH884ntw.about: I’m a film wedding photographer based out of Denver, CO, but I love to travel and will go wherever your love takes me! A few things you should know about me: I’m a Twilight and Harry Potter fanatic, I have killed every plant I’ve ever owned, and you’ll often find me in a coffee shop or snuggled up on my couch with a good book. (And by “good” I of course mean either fantasy or trashy romance). “You just have the ability to capture people’s essences. Every photo you take feels so authentic and personal .” On your wedding day, there is nothing more important to me than ensuring that you are able to be fully present in the moment . This day should be all about celebrating your and your partner’s love with your favorite people. This should be a day of unfiltered joy, of dancing until your feet hurt, of radiant smiles, happy tears, and a whole lotta kisses. Your day is NOT a photoshoot. It is not an opportunity for me to get cool pictures for Instagram. My job is to serve you . I do so by silently observing , guiding where it’s needed, but ultimately being as hands-off as possible so that you’re able to spend your wedding day solely focused on enjoying this time with your loved ones , rather than worrying about spending hours of your day taking photos. ChIJy6-WMP9_a4cRK4kP0aveJYY.home: Two Generations. One Passion for Storytelling. Every person, family, business, and organization has a story worth telling. At Sandy Puc Productions, storytelling is more than what we do; it's who we are. As a mother-and-son creative team, Sandy and Nikolai Puc bring together decades of experience, fresh perspective, and a shared passion for creating films that connect, inspire, and endure. From heartfelt documentaries and powerful brand stories to commercial productions, weddings, and life celebrations, every project is crafted with purpose and authenticity. Sandy has spent more than three decades helping people tell their stories through photography and film. Whether we're documenting a family's most cherished moments, producing a campaign for a growing business, or traveling across the globe to tell stories that make a difference, our mission remains the same: Create work that people don't just watch, they remember.
